reading.rtitle: Six Weeks to the First Live Show
paras: Every season of a singing show starts with a calendar. In January, the music director meets the producers to plan the upcoming season. The first live show is on the twelfth of April, and nothing is going to move that date. So the team works backwards from it. This year, they are going to record all the backing tracks in their own studio, and they are going to start a month earlier than last year.

The first weeks are full of tentative plans. A studio slot is penciled in for the second week of February, but it is not confirmed yet. The band is coming in on the fifteenth, and the director is meeting the vocal coaches on the following Monday. Those dates are firm: people have agreed to them, and they are in everybody's calendar.

Then, in the middle of February, something goes wrong, as it does every year. This time, the studio slot clashed with a recording for another show. The producer looked at the calendar and said, "We are going to fall behind if we lose this week." The music director did not wait. "I'll call the studio myself," she said. "And I'll ask the band to come in on Saturday." Two hours later, the new dates were firmed up.

Now the team is on track. Twenty arrangements are due by the end of March, and the last ones will probably arrive a few days late, because they always do. But the director is calm. "We'll wrap everything up before the first rehearsal," she says. "I'm sure of it." After fifteen seasons, she knows the difference between a plan, an arrangement and a promise.

tips: I'm meeting a producer at three.

listenings.text: Next week is the busiest week of the season, so let me tell you how it is going to work. On Monday, I'm meeting the six singers who are still in the competition. Each of them is getting forty minutes with me, one by one. On Tuesday and Wednesday, we are rehearsing with the band, and on Thursday the camera team is coming in for a full run-through. Friday is tentative. If everything is on track, we are going to give the singers the day off, because tired voices make mistakes. If not, we will use Friday to fix what is still not working. One singer has a sore throat right now, so I am going to keep her rehearsals short. I don't know yet who will win on Saturday. But I know one thing: they will all be ready.

In September, I'm starting an online course in music production. I have a full-time job in television, so I have to be realistic. I'm not going to study every night. That plan never works. Instead, I'm going to study three mornings a week, before work, from six to eight. My first assignment is due on the twentieth, and I have already penciled in a session with a friend who plays the drums. We are recording on a Sunday, because that is the only day when the studio is free. Will it be easy? Probably not. I think I will fall behind in the first month, because everybody does. But I have a calendar, I have a plan, and I have a reason. And when it gets hard, I'll remember why I started.
